newsitem.title: CHINA: China central bank chief defends interest cuts.
newsitem.headline: China central bank chief defends interest cuts.

text.p: China's central bank governor Dai Xianglong defended on Tuesday two interest rate cuts this year, saying these were not a sign the bank would relax monetary policy.
Speaking to an international business conference, he also said retail prices would rise by about 7.0 percent this year and annual economic growth would be about 10 percent.
"The two interest rate cuts were made under the condition of falling prices," said Dai, head of the People's Bank of China.
"Therefore one cannot draw the conclusion that the central bank will relax monetary policy."
China cut interest rates in May and again in August in response to falling inflation.
Retail price inflation was a year-on-year 5.8 percent in August and official figures on Tuesday showed consumer price inflation at 8.1 percent.

China has set a target of 10 percent inflation for 1996, down from 14.8 percent last year, and officials have identified battling inflation as a top priority since the retail index raced to a communist-era record of 21.7 percent in 1994.
Dai said monetary policy during the current 1996-2000 five-year plan should be neither too lax nor too tight.
"A relatively tight monetary policy should continue to be pursued," he said. "Control of inflation should be regarded as the primary task in macro-economic adjustment...in the financial sector."

China clamped a squeeze on credit in mid-1993 to try to cool inflation and rein in an overheating economy. But it has shown signs of easing in recent months, especially in the face of pleas from lumbering state-owned firms hard-hit by the austerity measures and unprepared for the sink-or-swim marketplace.

Dai said the broad M2 money supply would rise by about 23 percent a year through the year 2000 while M1, which tallies currency in circulation and current deposits, would climb by about 18 percent a year over the period.
China has set targets of 25 percent and 18 percent for M2 and M1 for all of this year.

China's economic growth topped 9.0 percent in the first eight months of the year, Dai said, adding that he expected gross domestic product to increase by about 10 percent for the whole year. China's GDP grew by 10.2 percent last year.
The central bank chief also said China's foreign exchange reserves had risen to more than $93 billion as of the end of August, up from $90.7 billion in early August.
Officials have said reserves could near $100 billion by the end of this year.
